label: Curves in 3-Space
notes: This short act, printed pages 106 through 108, asks a single question: what new information appears once a curve is free to leave a plane? Plane curves carried one scalar, curvature. In space we need a second scalar, torsion, plus a moving frame to register both.

label: From Plane Curves to Space Curves
notes: In the plane a curve bends but cannot escape its page, so one number per point suffices. A space curve can additionally lift out of any plane we draw it against. We contrast a flat circle with a climbing spring, asking what extra invariant that climb encodes.

label: Unit-Speed Parameterization
notes: Before measuring bending we strip away how fast the curve is traced. Reparameterizing by arc length makes the velocity a unit tangent, so every later derivative reports pure geometry rather than the bookkeeping of speed. Arc length is intrinsic; the original parameter is merely a label.

label: The Unit Tangent and Curvature
notes: Differentiating the unit tangent gives a vector orthogonal to it whose length is the curvature kappa. Kappa measures how sharply the tangent direction swings per unit length. We tie this to the osculating circle of radius one over kappa, the round arc that best hugs the curve.

label: The Frenet Frame
notes: At each point we attach three orthonormal vectors: the tangent pointing along motion, the principal normal pointing toward the center of bending, and the binormal completing a right-handed triple. This moving frame travels with the particle and turns studying a curve into studying how its frame rotates.

label: The Osculating Plane
notes: The tangent and normal span the osculating plane, the flat sheet that locally contains the curve to second order. The binormal is its unit perpendicular. For a plane curve this sheet never moves, so any change in the binormal signals the curve leaving its plane.

label: Torsion: Twisting Out of the Plane
notes: Torsion tau measures how fast the osculating plane rotates about the tangent as we advance along the curve. Equivalently it is the rate at which the binormal tips. Curvature records bending within a plane; torsion records the curve corkscrewing out of that plane into the third dimension.

label: The Frenet-Serret Equations
notes: The derivatives of the three frame vectors against arc length obey a single skew-symmetric matrix built from kappa and tau. The tangent turns toward the normal, the binormal turns toward the normal, and the normal feeds both back. Skew-symmetry keeps the frame orthonormal as it rotates rigidly.

label: Reading the Frame as Rotation
notes: The skew-symmetric coefficient matrix is the angular velocity of the frame, the Darboux vector. Its component along the binormal is curvature and its component along the tangent is torsion. The whole motion of the frame is one instantaneous rotation, cleanly decomposed into bending and twisting parts.

label: The Helix: Constant Curvature and Torsion
notes: A circular helix has constant curvature and constant torsion, and conversely those two constants determine a helix up to rigid motion. It is the model space curve, the analogue of the circle for plane curves. Explicit radius and pitch formulas express kappa and tau directly.

label: The Fundamental Theorem of Space Curves
notes: Prescribing curvature and torsion as functions of arc length determines a curve uniquely up to a rigid motion of space. Kappa and tau are therefore a complete set of bending-and-twisting invariants. This is the payoff: two scalars fully encode the shape of any space curve.

label: Recap and the Straw Model
notes: We close with the physical straw-and-wire picture: thread a bent wire through straws and watch the frame ride along it. Recapping, kappa bends the curve inside the osculating plane and tau twists that plane about the tangent, and together they replay the entire curve, setting up surfaces ahead.
